utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. I was dealing with the Defence submissions regarding crimes at the camp. And may I begin, as it were, at the end of the indictment against Isak Musliu first with the two counts of murder that he faces in Counts 7 and 8. And can I deal first with the alleged murder of Ajet Gashi, who was according to L-64 executed at an intersection outside of the camp. Alushani, according to him, tells him, L-64, that they have orders to execute Ajet Gashi, which is according to L-64 precisely what Alushani and Tamuli then did. We put our case here very simply: There is no evidence of any involvement by Isak Musliu personally in the death of Ajet Gashi before, during, or after his death, none. Fehmi Tafa. L-10 said and gave evidence that this victim was dragged out of a room by Messrs. Bala and Musliu. 20 minutes later he is dragged back in and 10 minutes or so after that he dies. In the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, it is alleged that it was Mr. Bala and Mr. Musliu who dragged him back into the room to die. This victim died, we now understand, as a result of a bullet wound to the thorax predominantly. Until that was known, we also proceeded on the basis that he was beaten to death. L-06, also in that room, gives a different account of the removal of Fehmi Tafa. That account does not involve either Mr. Musliu nor, indeed, Mr. Bala but two others altogether: Ramadan Behluli and Ali Gashi. L-06 had those same two men return the victim to the room. L-10, as we've just observed, gives a version involving the removal of this particular victim by the two masked men he identifies as Qerqiz and another, was actually his answer. It's worth noting that of Qerqiz L-10 also said this, and the transcript reference for Your Honours' note is 2.949, and I quote: "I don't know how people over there identified him, but this person all the time wore a mask. "Q. How could you distinguish Qerqiz from other soldiers or people you saw? "A. I probably would not be able to tell because he was wearing a mask." He was to go on to tell you that he had heard Qerqiz had become a policeman and he'd heard that his real name was Isak Musliu. It was L-10, you will recall, who went on in evidence to speak of meetings and conversations with L-96. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: (redacted) Curious. I put it no higher than that. The accounts are, we suggest, however, irreconcilable with each other and most certainly not sufficiently clear and compatible with the grave, gravest, of all allegations made against Isak Musliu. So Jefta Petkovic and Zvonko Marinkovic, two more murder victims, it is said of Isak Musliu, said by L-04 to have been removed from the cowshed by Mr. Musliu. As we understand the totality of the evidence in this case, no other witness gave any other evidence of Musliu's involvement. In five pre-trial interviews, L-04 had given no descriptions of Isak Musliu. The best it gets is when he's shown U-1, the photo spread by Mr. Kereakes and says: "He looks familiar." The man he knew as Qerqiz was always masked. Asked why in his interview on the 16th of January, 2002, in which he gave car registration numbers and named no fewer than 16 people. He did not name Qerqiz. His reply was, and I quote: "I don't remember anyone asking me." This evidence, we suggest, falls very short, very far short of the standard required to found any allegation, still less one of murder. Agim Ademaj and Vesel Ahmeti. Kidnapped on the 27th of June, 1998, it is said, along with Shyqyri Zymeri. Last seen alive, it is said, when, according to L-04, they were taken away by Isak Musliu. Precisely the same submissions are made here as in relation to the preceding cases. And finally Sinisa Blagojevic. Now it is said, of course, and it is accepted that there is no evidence to implicate Isak Musliu in this killing. So how do we put it in the round? In the round we put it very simply indeed: There is either no nor sufficiently credible and reliable evidence upon which this Chamber could begin to be satisfied so that it was sure of that it Musliu was involved in the murders pursuant to Article 7(1). Still looking at Defence submissions on crimes at the camp, and we move up the indictment, Counts 3 to 6 inclusive, dealing, as they do, with torture, inhumane acts, and treatment. Eight incidents are set out in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. We hope we've conveniently summarised them for you, and I don't go through them at paragraph 932 of the final Defence brief. But it is primarily, you will recollect, from four Prosecution witnesses, we suggest, come the allegations of Musliu mistreating prisoners. They are L-96 who makes, as I observed yesterday, direct identification, as it were, by way of recognition. And a combination of L-04, -10, and -12, all of whom allege mistreatment by Qerqiz of one kind or another. L-04 gave evidence that others identifying Qerqiz as their assailant while blindfolded, being beaten by Qerqiz and further gave evidence of, as I think he put it, daily beatings. But, but, he has never properly identified Isak Musliu as the man he knew as Qerqiz. I'm going to pause because I've obviously done something wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting is making all kinds of implicatory signs to me so it doesn't sound too terrible, but I apologise for whatever it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Oh, well, that is bad. I apologise. May I repeat the last point. L-04 has never, we suggest and we submit, properly identified Musliu as the man he knew as Qerqiz. Milaim Kamberi who, as again we observed yesterday, has not been called to give evidence before you is said to be the source of the name Musliu. At all times L-04 was to tell us the man Qerqiz was masked. It was L-04 who told investigators that a woman who beat L-12 was Qerqiz's sister. Well, when taxed about that, he revealed this was simply something told to him by a relative claiming, when further pressed on the subject, that he now did not remember the name nor remember implicating Qerqiz's sister. Your Honours, we submit yet again this evidence from this witness of this character woefully lacks the clarity and the certainty required to convict. And so I can move to L-10 who spoke of the ongoing dispute with another family, a dispute he said that was: "Never revolved," I repeat, "never resolved." Qerqizi was one who mistreated them, he said. He gave, did L-10, an account of the beating of Emin Emini by Qerqizi and others. L-06, he said, was also taken out by three men. L-06 himself gave a different account of his own beating, namely that it was at 11.00: "Ramadan Behluli and Ali Gashi who took me blindfolded me and took me to the manure."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber here perhaps have examples that we've just been dealing with of witnesses who may well be doing their honest best but who are not, for wholly understandable reasons, either accurate or reliable, either taken individually or together or at least sufficiently accurate or reliable for the specific purpose for which you need them. And likewise with L-12. He claimed to have been beaten by someone called Rahman Qerqiz, Rahman Qerqiz. As to Qerqizi he said: "Yes, I've heard the name but I don't know who the person was. When asked when he'd heard the name, it got even vaguer. "I don't know who was there. I don't know who the person was." The family dispute he confirmed that his family was having with another. He said about it this, interestingly you may think. "Of course," he said, "there must have been some links to it," the "it" being their taking away and their detention. As to this man Rahman, he said this: "He did what he had to do." Rahman said: "You thought you'd never fall into my hands." What's happened here? Could he be confused? Could he be meaning to say that it was not Rahman Qerqiz but Ramadan into whose hands he fell? Does that not explain that remark made to him? Is not this an old score being settled and not a policy being carried out? That's a matter for you. But returning finally to L-12. You may think when reviewed that his evidence in reality takes the case against him, Musliu, that is, no further. Well, L-96 falls into a rather different category. We haven't said much about him yet, and I'm just going to put that right in the next few minutes. If, in your view, L-96 is honest, accurate, and reliable, you will have gone a good way to convict Isak Musliu in respect of at least a fraction of this indictment, namely one beating. And I'm going to stop because I've obviously transgressed again. Is it the same transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's private session testimony that was quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I didn't think I put a name to it. My apologies. We submit about L-96 that carefully and fairly analysed there is just too much doubt surrounding aspects of him and his evidence to leave you anything like sure enough that he's honest, accurate, and reliable. Although he claimed to the contrary, we suggest that he and possibly other members of his family had some relationship with the Serb authorities. And we'll come to it much later on. (redacted) (redacted) We suggest his denial of a boycott of his family in 1992 was not true, as is his denial of providing detailed information voluntarily to Jasovic and Sparavalo in his interview with them before his detention at Lapusnik. And may I just interpose a point here about Jasovic and Sparavalo. Despite all we now know about both of them and their activities, it must have been possible for them to have conducted at least some interviews which led to accurate statements being freely made. They cannot, you may think, have tortured or threatened everyone, especially those for whom, for one reason or another, were assisting them willingly but who would never, ever subsequently admit to doing so. We suggest that L-96's denial of even knowing Momcilo Sparavalo as state security, who made a statement to this Tribunal claiming at least some kind of friendly, social relationship with him and his family was again untrue. We suggest, therefore, that for L-96 to have handed himself in to a Serb checkpoint after his escape from Berisa is precisely what he would do. The accounts he and Jasovic give of the circumstances surrounding and the contents of their two meetings are not reconcilable. We simply give you the references. If you'd be good enough in due course to compare L-96's version between 2.275 and 2.279 with Jasovic's spread over between 5.279 and 5.397, one of them, or both of them, is not being honest with this Tribunal, we submit. Of course, if he and his were or were thought of to be collaborators and/or informants, that would not of course legally justify, still less excuse, torture and murder - no one is suggesting otherwise, for it would be impossible to do so - however, it may go some way to explain why he might just might be prepared to fabricate allegations against, for example, Isak Musliu even in, even in, a somewhat restrained way. By a side wind and if one considers it carefully enough, we suggest he revealed a considerable animus towards Isak Musliu. When put to him that Musliu may have been in Rahovec for a period corresponding to his own detention, he responded by saying: "I'm convinced he never went out to fight. What he could do was to find someone, tie them up, and beat them. That's what I think." He accuses Musliu, you may think, in that short passage therefore of gross cowardice and makes a corresponding allegation against him before you. Are these old scores being settled? Is this what he believes? Is his animus towards parts of the KLA finding an outlet? But he failed to mention Musliu, a man he knew and could identify easily, either to Serbs in August 1998, and at trial he said neither to UNMIK in his first statement to them is, we suggest, both extraordinary and indicative. Indicative perhaps of a witness who is waiting for information, for gossip, for intelligence, call it what you will, before carelessly - and I use that word in its strict sense - passing it on. Extraordinary perhaps because he's speaking of what his relative had told him just minutes, moments before his relative died. He claims his relative spoke of Qerqiz and said so I was focussed on Shala and Qerqiz. And as to descriptions, it is remarkable, we submit, that he does not give Isak Musliu a beard until he gets to this Tribunal. Why? He wasn't asked, he said. So finally and in conclusion regarding L-96, overruling the Prosecution's objection to our attempt to extract an apology from him to Agim Murtezi, L-96 refused to apologise. He'd lost a relative. He has perhaps lost other connections in his homeland, perhaps forever. He has every reason to be bitter and vengeful. His place in his homeland may have been compromised by a connection to or affiliation with elements of the Serb regime which were long-standing and deep-seated. Others, others have given signed statements to this Tribunal calling him an untruthful man, a liar. Xheladin Ademaj, for one, for someone who cannot always be believed; Hyzri, for another, in our 92 bis material. Before and after his detention he was with Jasovic. There is, we submit, just too much here for the Trial Chamber to be anything other than dubious at best and doubtful at least regarding parts of his testimony, if not most of it. We can't put it more plainly and more simply: No conviction would be safe based on the evidence of this witness. So we move to the top of the indictment in Counts 1 and 2: Imprisonment and cruel treatment. L-96, with whom we've just dealt with and about whom we have no more to say, are relevant here -- is relevant here and so of course is L-64 giving evidence regarding this as well as other aspects. And of L-64 the Prosecution say to you, highly reliable and should be credited by the Trial Chamber; paragraph 88 of their brief. Well, may we spend a moment or two on L-64, who warrants some attention. If, if, there were rogue elements within the KLA acting without proper command or control, carrying out acts independently, and if the evidence is, as indeed it is, that Musliu was no part of them, and if they carried out any of the acts with which we are here concerned, then that should, we suggest, impinge and impinge significantly on your deliberations. Well, there are two parts to that short series of questions, as it were. First of all: Rogue elements, did they exist? Yes, they did. Who says so? Jan Kickert said so and he said so before you on the 23rd of November of last year. Referring to "breakaway KLA factions," he called them. He said at page 676 of the transcript: "There was a general problem I ... assessed at the time ... in western Kosovo there was some armed group who would ... do their own thing and not necessarily follow any ... command." Susanne Ringgaard Pedersen, of whom we've already spoken, too spoke of rogue elements. The second aspect of the questions we pose regarding this area: "Did they carry out any acts with which you are concerned? "A. Well, that's the crucial question." If there was a prime candidate for membership of a group of rogues, it was L-64. Where and with whom does he end up? He ends up in Lapusnik with Voglushi. Significant reliance is placed on this witness by the Prosecution. Examples of where he enters this case, literally from start to finish, he is central to their case against Isak Musliu. So it is from camp location to trenches and positions, from rules to oath ceremonies, from personal appearances to command responsibility, this witness occurs and recurs to testify against Isak Musliu. And as with L-96, you have to be sure that in relation to all matters of importance he is honest, accurate, and reliable. We suggest within the body of 595 pages of transcript of his evidence, there is a positive gold mine of riches to be excavated. For example, his character, his antecedents, his criminal activities, his violence, his dishonesty, his duplicity, his perjury before you have all, we suggest, been amply demonstrated. Who will ever forget his euphemism for murder to escort somebody? Is it to be seriously believed that he did not personally beat the feet of that poor Serb woman, feigning mental illness? The image of him sneaking rat-like into a room to lift the head of a man with rifle may live in the memory for a long time to come. Getting into that cowshed, Your Honours, was not like any of us in Defence bar getting into the United Nations Detention Unit down the road. You didn't have to show a passport or identification or wait for doors to be unlocked. You could, you may think, he did, you may think, just go in as he pleased, alone if necessary, if that is what was going on there. Look hard, if you will, at his account of being condemned for going to Lladroc to get weapons. Look hard, if you would, at his refusal to accept our suggestion that he was dismissed by Musliu, you wouldn't have this at all, for plotting a murder. You may recall it was the alleged plot to murder a man called Mziu, I don't know if I have pronounced that correctly, M-z-i-u. Within 29 pages of transcript, between pages 4.839 and 4.868, his evidence went from this: "I didn't go to kill him," to, "there was a plan to kill." Look hard, if you would, at his denials and interview in May 2003 to going to a prison, his admissions before you trying to wriggle that he may have only then been referring to a specific time frame. Test his assertion that he didn't maltreat anyone "with the exception of a slap." Prosecution say, Prosecution say, well, if he'd invented his testimony, he would have embellished his accounts. Well, he's subtler than that, much subtler than that. Consider whether he's quick-witted enough to pick up on a cue offered to him even before you. On travel permits, one is shown to him; our Exhibit P171. "Q. On this example it's signed by a commander. In Lapusnik, would it be signed by Qerqiz?" Well, good old leading question, that. "A. Yes, Qerqiz." Is L-64 really to be believed, believed and preferred, on note-making and note-taking to Ruzhdi Karpuzi? Prior to reaching Lapusnik and talking of his time in the earlier part of 1998 in a unit called Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Zjarri, Z-j-a-r-r-i, which I think means fire, he said this: "I didn't call myself a KLA soldier ... I felt I became ... a KLA soldier ... but for the above-mentioned reasons, I didn't admit it." What were those above-mentioned reasons? We did sporadic operations. Ymer would have formed this group with or without permission from Nekovce, he said, sporadic operations. His capacity for deviousness and dishonesty found no inhibition before you. Questioned by Mr. Whiting: "Do you remember" -- rather by me; forgive me. "Do you remember what you told him," Mr. Whiting, "last week what the word 'escort' meant?" His extraordinary answer to you, Your Honours, was: "It means to accompany somebody." It did not interest him to report to anyone that the wrong Murrizi was here accused. He was at best a foot soldier, ignorant in every sense of organisation and structure. He was a marksman and a thug. And so it is he would remember and remember well Zenel, Zeneli, another KLA soldier. I mentioned him yesterday. Zeneli spoke about his karate skills. There's another karate man in this plan, Lapusnik, at least one, and there he is, Zeneli. Could that be who L-07 was referring to? He is, we suggest, just the kind of person L-64, to hold a grudge against Musliu for dismissing him and would not think twice if he thought it would get him any advantage to fabricate allegations against his former group leader. That is what we suggest he's done or might have done. Given all you now know of him, can you safely and surely rely on him? We say: Simply not so. So we finish crimes at the camp. We've addressed you yesterday on command responsibility for those matters. And likewise and it follows, we suggest, that for all those same reasons that Musliu is not liable for crimes pursuant to Article 7(3) he cannot and, we submit, he should not be found to have participated in the joint criminal enterprise, assuming of course you find one proved. And with those words we conclude our analysis of the Prosecution's case, and I can move on, therefore, to the Defence case. Your Honours, I think, as I indicated yesterday, I will almost certainly finish before or by the first break. Reduced to its bare essentials, what is that case for Isak Musliu? Well, it comes down to six points. First of all, that in May he became the leader of a group of volunteers in Lapusnik; secondly, that group grew eventually before 25 July into Celiku 3, which itself was made up of five fighting positions for which he was given responsibility, and I forensically underline the words "fighting positions; thirdly, as Fatmir Limaj was to confirm, Musliu became the commander of Celiku 3 and post-August 16th deputy commander of the 121st Brigade; fourthly, there were other units under different commands in Lapusnik; there was not, our fifth point, an overall commander in Lapusnik; and finally in summary form his case is that beyond the limited detentions of which he spoke in his May 2001 interview, he had no knowledge of nor any involvement in any prison camp, neither did he command any soldier whom to his knowledge played any part in such a place. We invite you to read the totality - or I should say re-read - of his interviews in 2001, about which we've already commented at length yesterday. The essentials of that case I've just set out are all there, you may think, upon a careful reading of both of those interviews. And that's extraordinary, given when they were conducted. In support of his case, statements in written form have been admitted under the 92 bis procedure. And it may be helpful when Your Honours come to consider these addresses later. If I were now just to briefly summarise what they each have to say because, as it were, that will lead us into our final section of this speech and its closing. The witness Hafik Bajrami, DM8 is the reference, is the holder of a doctorate in military, political and social administration in Kosova. A history teacher, director of the Kosova archive, one-time president of the Mother Teresa organisation. He provides a detailed analysis of history, the history of oppression and discrimination suffered by the Albanians in Kosovo at the hands of the Serb regime. He sets out in paragraphs 44 to 47 illuminating and shocking statistics as to the cost in human terms of the situation in Kosovo between 1981 and 1999. It demonstrates, we suggest, as Colonel Crosland agreed before you, that one can legitimately describe the Serb regime approach in 1998 as being in and of itself a widespread and systematic attack upon Kosovar Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: (redacted) He speaks of a paucity of uniforms and ammunition. And from his standpoint, an insufficient command structure. (redacted) (redacted) I can say that he had close relationships, L-96, with Serbs. I saw him wearing uniform pants obtained from Serbs. And I've had no contact since 1996 or 1997, but in my opinion, in my opinion, based on my knowledge of L-96, he is not someone who can always be believed. DM15 is Raif Veliu, who is a 43-year-old Albanian. A non-combatant who has no knowledge of nor ever had any dealings with Isak Musliu. He speaks instead of L-96, so I deal with him slightly out of numerical turn now. (redacted) He, too, speaks quite independently of the previous witness, of L-96's rather strange and apparent interest in wearing Serb uniform, in order to make friends with Serbs, as he put it. L-96, he claims, would often be seen with and socialise with Serb police officers. No secret they were visitors to their home. Agim Kameri, a 39-year-old born in Racak and from 1994 president of the LDK in Racak, DM10. Post-war the mayor of Racak, a non-combatant. He was involved in the so-called civil directorate which carried out organisational support for civilian population. He's known Musliu since Musliu was a child. He recalls Musliu addressing a meeting in the mosque in Racak in 1998 for which he recalls Isak Musliu stressing the importance of the KLA respecting the civilian population and saying: We as an army are determined to fight against the occupying forces only. To him and to his co-villagers, Mr. Kameri tells you, Musliu is, as he puts it, a living hero. I feel proud to be a cohabitant of his from Racak. The entire village had good words and convictions about him, he says, where Mr. Musliu joined the KPS. Following the Racak massacre, which you know took place in January 1999, this witness was intimately involved in the aftermath. And of Mr. Musliu, he says, he was the only one who comforted us and kept us calm. We'd all lost all of our hopes. Under seal is a witness I shall simply refer to as DM11.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: (redacted) Described ethnic demarcation of the police beginning in May 1989, as a result of which he was dismissed for sometime, but in 1989 managed to get himself reinstated as chief executive of the director for public safety in Ferizaj. He knew Jasovic and Sparavalo. He knew them to maltreat and kill innocent civilians. He knew that they were taking and forcing statements out of detainees. He speaks, too, of their involvement in the notorious black hand organisation. He speaks of the bodies of state security, focussing attention on neutralising and paralysing, as he puts it, Albanian institutions and their policy of targeting the civilian population. He describes his own departure from the police force as an escape. He has been intimidated and threatened since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: (redacted) He, too, speaks of Jasovic mistreating and maltreating Albanians. Beatings would be carried out just for attending demonstrations. Ferizaj police station on the third floor was a favourite location for this kind of activity. Momcilo Sparavalo was, he says, an extremist, a person who was considered to be a nationalist extremist who was not supposed to be in the SUP, says this witness, but Sparavalo was. The statement goes on in great detail to catalogue unlawful and brutal conduct of Jasovic, Sparavalo, and other police and state security personnel. DM12, also under seal, (redacted) (redacted), speaks in very similar terms of the work of state security. Speaks, too, of Mika Sparavalo, the father of Momcilo Sparavalo, an extreme pair of nationalists. Goes on to deal with the former plumber, Dragan Jasovic and his violently despicable conduct as a police officer, his inability to stop him from what he was doing. Ismail Smajli is a 34-year-old from Carraleve and a former KLA soldier. June 1998 he joined and became one of the KLA in Rance where Zenel, Zeneli, was in charge, he recalls. He's known Musliu since his childhood. He speaks very highly of him, having a strong belief in the rule of law and as respecting the rights of all. This witness became a colleague in the police force in the KPS with Musliu in June or July 1999. He says he was distinguished and hard-working and successful as a police officer. His work would take him into the Serb community where he saw firsthand him providing security for Serb civilians. Shyqeri Salihu, a 45-year-old who joined the KLA in August 1998, became head of logistics in a village in the Pastrik zone. The two worked in the police force in the Nerodime zone with Musliu. He recalls in glowing terms Musliu's life-saving attempt of a Roma gypsy boy who in April 2002 fell into a freezing cold fast-flowing river. Off duty, Isak Musliu tried in duty and in vain to try and save the life of this child. This was typical of Isak, he said, constantly putting lives of community members above his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: (redacted) long statement from K5 who describes himself effectively as an informant. Describes in chilling detail how he joined the Serbian police force and was a hired hand to bomb and shoot selected Albanian targets. For some of his work, K5, as he's known, was provided with a KLA uniform and a Chinese Kalashnikov and Chinese hand-grenades. The object, of course, of the exercise, to deceive people into thinking that his attacks were in fact carried out by the KLA. And finally under seal DM19, a medical report which I just simply refer to and remind Your Honours of. And that's our summary in brief of the 92 bis material. The Chamber will not of course have forgotten a considerable body of material put in by Mr. Lehtinen regarding Mr. Musliu's work in the police force. In our final brief under the heading of background and current circumstances a number of matters are set out which are relevant, both to the issue of guilt insofar as they touch upon character and are plainly and would plainly be relevant in relation to sentence. And I commend them to the Tribunal upon those dual bases. He was dismissed, was Musliu, from the KPS as we see from the material Mr. Lehtinen provided for not being honest about his school qualifications. We respectfully submit that his dismissal, you may think, had rather more to do with his alleged participation in this indictment than whether he lied about how many exams he had taken. He is, we would submit, as we would submit in our own jurisdiction, a man of good character. He's demonstrated through the material before you a man, we would submit, of positive, good character. By his bearing and his conduct he has to many people demonstrated himself to be a hard-working, devoted family man, a calm man with a pleasant manner, a man caring of his community, a man prepared and willing to step from his community into others in a wholly positive and constructive way, the kind of man who would risk his life for a drowning Roma child. A man who believes in self control and discipline, a man who in war wanted to fight within the rules and against only other combatants, a man who respected the importance of protecting the civilian community, a man who was prepared to sacrifice his life in defence of the human rights of his people. Of course, good character, even positive good character, cannot by itself provide a defence to a criminal charge, but it is, we submit, evidence which you should take into account in his favour. He's chosen not to give evidence; that is and remains his right. He is, through us, entitled to sit there and stay silent and ask the Prosecution to prove its case against him. No adverse inferences can nor will be drawn against him by reason of his silence. The Chamber will not, of course, speculate as to why he neither gave nor called any evidence and neither, of course, will it speculate as to what he might have said or how he may have performed in the witness box. Comments made in the final address of the Prosecution earlier this week regarding the alibi that failed to materialise does not alter the position as we've sought just now to characterise it. And, Your Honours, in any event, would being in Rahovec be an alibi for not being in Lapusnik? Look at the map. So it is that we've reached the end of what we wish to say, and I just want to make one or two closing remarks. And I'll wait while people just keep walking in front of me. It's a bit distracting. When Mr. Cayley concluded his opening to you on the 15th of November last he said this: "I must now let the evidence speak." Well, spoken it has over 80-odd days stretching back over 10 months with a transcript filling 15 or so ring-binders as well as a considerable amount of documentary and visual and audio material. If it was right to observe that -- at the outset that the essential facts of this case are "straightforward and compelling," we suggest that when it comes to reaching a verdict in our client's case, "straightforward" will not be the word to use. As, Your Honours, this will be the last you'll hear from the bar in this trial, may I just be permitted to say one or two things. First of all, please forgive our sometimes lame attempts at humour. This has not -- or this has, rather, been for us as it has for Your Honours, as for everyone in this room, our workplace for the last ten months and a workplace would be a sad place were it not for the occasional smile. But nothing can nor will retract from the seriousness of the solemn task we've sought to perform and the one that still lies ahead for Your Honours. We would wish to thank all who have assisted us in court, from the registry, from Chambers, court ushers, and prisoner officers who have all patiently and good humouredly put up with us. We would wish to thank and pay particular tribute to the many interpreters who have been with us, both behind the glass and in court, with whom we literally could not have functioned. And finally, a limitless amount of thanks goes to all those who have assisted Mr. Mansfield, Mr. Guy-Smith, myself, Mr. Harvey, and myself, and Mr. Powles, in Kosovo and here; our legal assistants, again without whom little or nothing could have been achieved. It's been our privilege to represent Isak Musliu and to defend him before Your Honours, whose patience has sustained us all. We do suggest this won't be easy. We have, we submit, climbed that mountain that we set ourselves to climb yesterday afternoon at about ten to 3.00. We've reached the top, we can look down, and we do say that the case against him has not been proved beyond reasonable doubt. So after all these weeks, after all these months, after all these documents, after all these words, we and he and they will wait patiently for just two more from Your Honours: Not guilty. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Topolski. I don't believe there's any other matter currently before the Chamber. That being so, may I thank counsel for the competence and care which they have undoubtedly given to this case. The Chamber has been greatly assisted. The proceedings have been able to be conducted more speedily and more efficiently because of the efforts of counsel. I would thank you, Mr. Topolski, for your appreciation of the work given by so many who, not centre stage, nevertheless whose efforts are essential for the functioning of this Chamber and this Tribunal. We have of course to now consider the case. As has been indicated by counsel, there is a great deal which has to be looked at with care. For that purpose, we must reserve our decision and will reach those decisions as soon as we can properly and carefully do so. The hearing is closed.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.21 p.m.
